source: Foster et al. (Meta FAIR) (2026) AI Research Preference Models
finding: Frozen pretrained LLMs, with no fine-tuning, choose which of several candidate research solutions to execute. Prompting only: they read plans, code and past executed results. This lifts a research agent on AIRS-Bench. It is the first direct test of a scaffold (not weights) for choosing what to run (gap 1).
numbers: Average normalized score 0.684 (unguided) to 0.711 (inference-only RPM) and 0.729 (agentic RPM with pilots). Validation-oracle ceiling 0.748, test-oracle 0.759. Probability of improvement 0.5923 and 0.5913, 95% CI lower bounds 0.5066 and 0.5018. The 24 h baseline score was reached in 14.88 h (inference-only) and 15.50 h (agentic): about 1.6x speedup, under two-thirds of the budget. Selection advantage vs final score: Pearson r=0.55, Spearman 0.56.
quote: the primary lever on research progress becomes research preference
limits: Candidates are ML solutions with a numeric validation score, not open research questions. Gains are modest (+0.027 and +0.045) and probability of improvement only about 0.59. One lab. No equal-token comparison against best-of-N or against fine-tuned judges.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only judge that sees the history of executed results beats no judge at equal run count. This supports an S0 gate that reads past question-outcome pairs. Gap 1 is only partly closed because no equal-token comparison with fine-tuned judges exists.

source: Foster et al. (2026) AI Research Preference Models: offline selection accuracy and pilot ablations
finding: Offline pairwise selection accuracy: inference-only judge about 61 to 65%, agentic judge with small pilot experiments about 78 to 84%. More history, more candidates and more reasoning all help. Pilots give a large gain for minutes of compute, which answers gap 2 for ML tasks.
numbers: Inference-only: accuracy 60.7 to 65.0% as history grows; single frontier models 64.66 to 67.44%; majority vote 68.04%; LLM-arbiter ensemble 69.35%. Agentic with pilots: 78.52% at 5 min, 82.78% at 30 min, 84.02% at 4 h. Validation-score oracle baseline 66.73%. Pilot tactics: reduced CV, subsampled data (full data was more reliable than subsampling), fewer epochs. Up to 30 pilots per decision. 15 suggestions per selection; the oracle advantage rises with pool size.
limits: Offline set built from the agent's own search trees on ML tuning tasks with fast numeric proxies. End-to-end runs used 5 min pilots because 4 h is too costly. Pilots share the agent's time budget, so early progress is slower.
agent_relevance: A 5-minute probe adds about 13 accuracy points over pure reasoning, 30 min about 18. Returns diminish after minutes. Design the S0 probe as minutes of compute, not hours.

source: Tong et al. (2026) Scientific Judge: scaling and out-of-domain transfer (re-read for gap 1)
finding: Trained citation-preference judges improve with data and transfer partly across fields, but all gains need weights. Data scaling is about log-linear.
numbers: Overall score rises 58.1 to 77.3 (Qwen3-4B) and 69.7 to 82.7 (Qwen3-30B-A3B) from base to final checkpoint (Section 4.2). Table 3 in-domain 64.7 to 80.9 and 71.7 to 83.1. Table 5 CS-only training: out-of-domain fields gain roughly +9 to +21 points (the table is garbled in text extraction; per-field cells not verified). Thinker win rates 81.5% and 76.5% in-domain, 83.0% and 76.0% out-of-domain.
limits: Labels are citation counts, so this judges 'will be cited', not 'is worth pursuing'. Fine-tuned weights, not a scaffold. Table cells unreliable; only prose numbers used.
agent_relevance: Sets the target for gap 1: a scaffold needs about 70 to 80% pairwise accuracy to match trained judges, while prompted base models sit near 58 to 70% on the same set.

source: Schopf and Farber (2026) Is this Idea Novel? RINoBench
finding: Even when given the idea AND its cited related works (retrieval already done), frontier LLMs judge novelty poorly against human expert scores. Their written justification matches human reasoning, but the number does not.
numbers: 1,381 ideas from OpenReview reviews, 5-point rubric (1,104 train, 277 test). Best macro-F1 17.2 (GPT-5), o3 16.2, others about 9.5 to 14.6. Per-class F1 is 0.0 on category 1 and 0 to 16.7 on category 2. Mean absolute error about 0.93 to 1.04. Justification alignment about 85 to 90; hallucination rates mostly under 5%.
quote: LLM-generated reasoning closely mirrors human rationales, this alignment does not reliably translate into accurate novelty judgments
limits: Gold labels are reviewer text rewritten by an LLM, then quality filtered. Related works are the paper's own cited works (title and abstract), so it tests judging with given context, not search. Reviewer novelty ratings are themselves noisy.
agent_relevance: Retrieval depth alone does not fix novelty scoring. A cheap check should output 'which prior work overlaps' (which matches humans) and not a scalar novelty score.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) OpenNovelty: agentic system for verifiable novelty assessment
finding: Four-phase pipeline: extract contributions, retrieve (top-50 core-task papers and up to 10 per contribution), build a taxonomy from titles and abstracts, then full-text claim-level comparison with verbatim evidence quotes. No ablation of full text vs abstract or of retrieval depth is reported; the text lists such evaluation as planned.
numbers: Retrieval: Top-K up to 10 papers per contribution; top-50 core-task papers for the taxonomy; temporal filter and self-reference removal. No cost curve or accuracy numbers found in the text.
limits: System description, not a controlled test. Cannot serve as evidence on cost versus catch rate. Has prompt-injection defences for full-text input.
agent_relevance: A plausible design (abstract-level triage, then full text only for a few top candidates), but the gap 3 cost curve is still unmeasured.

source: Mostafa, Nguyen, Ahmadi (2026) Are We Truly Innovating? Originality in AI research papers
finding: Built on over 100,000 peer-review reports. General-purpose LLMs overestimate originality and collapse predictions to moderate or high scores. A fine-tuned model with retrieval does better; retrieval adds a small gain over the same model without it. Baselines struggle with paraphrased copies.
numbers: Table 1 ablation: Novelty Reviewer without retrieval 0.73, full framework 0.76 (metric column not confirmed from extraction); baselines Paper Reviewer 0.41, OpenReviewer 0.14. Plagiarism case: 10 papers from 2023, paraphrased; the retrieval model recognised far more originals than baselines (counts not verified). Also tested on MIDL 2026 (medical imaging), an unseen venue.
limits: Fine-tuned model, not a prompt scaffold. The 10-case plagiarism study is tiny. The metric name for 0.73 vs 0.76 was not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Retrieval adds about +0.03 on top of a trained judge; most of the gain is from training that fixes novelty inflation. A scaffold needs a calibration step: assume the idea is known until shown new.

source: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave, Ulrich (2026) AI and its impact on creativity and diversity: LLM-generated product ideas
finding: Outside NLP research (gap 4): product ideas for college students under 50 dollars, judged by consumer purchase intent, a market-style outcome proxy. LLM ideas have higher mean quality and more top-decile ideas but are less novel and less diverse as a set.
numbers: Purchase intent: human 40.4%, GPT-4 zero-shot 46.4%, few-shot 49.3% (B=0.059 and 0.089, p<.001). Top 10% of 400 ideas (40 ideas): 5 human, 15 zero-shot, 20 few-shot. Novelty: human 40.6%, LLM 36.7% and 36.1% (p=.008). Novelty vs purchase intent r=-0.078 (n.s.). Rephrasing check: no purchase-intent difference. Abstract: AI ideas 7 times more likely in top 10%. Diversity partly restored by pooling vendors, personas, chain-of-thought, creative agents; scaling idea count approaches human coverage of 200 human ideas.
limits: Product ideas, one market, GPT-4-era models, online panel (AI contamination estimated about 4% or below). Accepted July 2026 after two revisions.
agent_relevance: Supports a generate-many-then-select-on-an-outcome-proxy rule outside science. Novelty and quality are nearly uncorrelated here, so keep a novelty gate and a value gate as separate checks.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Ideation Arena: battle-style human expert assessment of LLM research ideas
finding: Large pairwise expert study (105 CS researchers, over 6,000 votes, 14 LLMs and 5 agent frameworks, shared closed context). Two experts agree on the winner only about 55 to 57% of the time and LLM judges top out at 72.56%. Agent frameworks help some base models a lot and others little.
numbers: Double-reviewed 1,675 queries (3,888 battles): pairwise agreement 56.8% overall quality, 54.4% novelty, 53.8% feasibility, 56.5% significance, 55.9% specificity; Krippendorff alpha about 0.59 to 0.61. LLM judge soft-accuracy on overall quality 59.52% (GPT-4o) to 72.56% (best); random 50.6 to 51.9%. Judge order swap Spearman 0.942. Leaderboard stable: Spearman 0.980 (50% annotator subsample) and 0.998 (leave-one-domain-out). AI-Researcher + DeepSeek V3.2 +177 Elo over the same base. Biology and Physics pilots: 4 experts each, pairwise agreement 0.539 and 0.556. Raters favoured long, mathematically specific proposals.
limits: Proposal-stage only, no execution. Computer science main benchmark. Ties scored half.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: with about 55% pairwise agreement, per-item labels from one expert are close to noise; stable rankings need thousands of votes. Gap 8: agent frameworks do not all beat their base model, so test each against the bare model.

source: Gottweis et al. (Google) (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist: Elo versus ground-truth accuracy and expert preference
finding: Tests gap 8 against an independent outcome. The tournament Elo (LLM-judged, not using ground truth) rises with accuracy on GPQA diamond questions; picking the top-Elo answer gives 78.4%. Evolution and meta-review agents add measurable gains. The expert evaluation is small.
numbers: GPQA diamond: top-Elo selection top-1 accuracy 78.4%; evolution agent raises precision 70.9% to 75.4% and auto-quality 4.7 to 5.6; meta-review raises AUC for correct solution 0.521 to 0.597. Expert study: 11 of 15 goals; Co-Scientist average preference rank 2.36, novelty 3.64, impact 3.09 out of 5. Two independent rater groups on NIH-style aims: Spearman rho 0.745.
limits: The paper itself says Elo is auto-evaluated and not ground truth. Accuracy vs Elo is compared only to a Gemini 2.0 reference with 32 samples per question. Only 15 goals; clinician pre-screening. No equal-token plain best-of-N baseline in the text read.
agent_relevance: Self-play ranking tracks correctness on questions that have an answer (GPQA), a different task from choosing open questions. Equal-token comparison with simple resampling is still missing, so gap 8 stays partly open.

source: Hill et al. (2025) The pivot penalty in research (Nature)
finding: Tests gap 6. The pivot penalty is only partly a reputation or audience effect. Holding the researcher's journal and field fixed cuts it about 26%, but most remains. It persists at every career stage, team size, and with or without new co-authors.
numbers: 25.8 million papers 1970-2015, 154 fields, top-5% hit rate. Within-journal comparison: coefficient about 26% less steep. Penalty about 1.6% steeper per year of career age, but present very early in careers. Patent citations fall 43% from lowest to highest pivot vigintile. Persists for big and small teams, new and existing co-authors, and COVID-19 pivots (impact premium largely offset).
quote: a pervasive 'pivot penalty', in which the impact of new research steeply declines the further a researcher moves
limits: Observational. Citations mix quality and audience reach. Pivot size is measured by change in cited-journal mix, not directly by lost expertise.
agent_relevance: About a quarter of the penalty is audience and reputation; the rest looks like lost local knowledge and fit. An agent lacks the reputation part, so switching is cheaper for it, but only if it can load the missing domain context. Keep a context-loading cost in the S0 switch rule.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster, Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery (PNAS)
finding: Full text opened (gap 5). A generative network model of problem choice, fitted to MEDLINE chemistry links. The observed strategy is near-optimal only for the first 10% of the network and increasingly inefficient beyond about 30%. Publishing failures and more risk-taking speed discovery.
numbers: Efficiency curves for random choice, the inferred MEDLINE strategy, and optimal strategies for 20%, 50% and 100% of the network. Quote-level: 'nearly optimal for discovering 10%', 'increasingly inefficient for more than 30%'. Optimal parameters from simulated annealing and MCMC. Failures are unpublished in the base scenario.
limits: A parameter setting for a network-growth task, not a risky-vs-safe fraction under a token budget. Assumes error-free experiments and a known full network. No 'x% risky' figure.
agent_relevance: The right mix depends on how much is already mapped. The agent's exploration share should rise as the explored share of its space rises, and failed attempts should be stored as shared memory. No fixed fraction is supported.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies (ASR), arXiv version
finding: Carried over from earlier evidence b08 (not re-opened here): 'new' and 'jump' strategies earn more citations on average (11.00 and 12.90 vs 8.38) but not enough to offset their lower success probability.
numbers: Break-even: p(new)=0.76 p(repeat) and p(jump)=0.65 p(repeat); mean citations 8.38 repeat, 11.00 new, 12.90 jump.
limits: Individual-level payoff, not system-level. Citations as value proxy. Not re-opened this session.
agent_relevance: For gap 5: a usable per-question rule. Take a risky question only if the probe puts its success probability above about 0.65 to 0.76 of the safe option's.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: cost of an outcome-based gold label
finding: Carried over from earlier evidence plus search summary: 43 experts each executed ideas, 100+ hours per idea, so a trustworthy outcome label is expensive (at least 4,300 expert-hours).
numbers: AI ideas lost 1.05 to 1.98 review points after execution vs 0.01 to 0.63 for human ideas (a05). 43 executed ideas, 100+ hours each. Direct post-execution comparison not significant (FDR 0.175 to 0.586).
limits: Carried over; not re-read this session. Underpowered for its own pre-registered hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: an executed gold set costs about 100 hours per item. Prefer cheap automatic outcome tasks with a number (as in d01) over expert execution.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Idea-level retrieval for novelty detection (search summary only)
finding: Search summary only: plain retrieve-then-cross-check pipelines fall short because text similarity misses conceptual similarity; the authors distil idea-level knowledge into a light retriever and release a benchmark.
limits: Only a search summary seen. Do not rely on it.
agent_relevance: Suggests rewriting the idea as a mechanism summary before retrieving on it; to be tested for gap 3.

source: Mixed-source note on expert agreement: Ideation Arena vs Si et al. vs Co-Scientist
finding: Ideation Arena states its 56.8% pairwise agreement is comparable to Si et al. (56.1% balanced accuracy). Two independent studies agree that two experts pick the same winner only slightly more than half the time. Rubric scores agree better than forced choice.
numbers: 56.8% (Ideation Arena, 1,675 queries) vs 56.1% (Si 2024). Co-Scientist rater groups on NIH-style aims: Spearman rho 0.745 on rubric scores. Biology and Physics pilots 0.539 and 0.556.
limits: Pairwise forced choice differs from rubric rating; rho and pairwise accuracy are not comparable measures.
agent_relevance: Gold labels: average rubric scores over 3 to 5 raters, or use outcomes with a number. One expert preference per item is not reliable.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting empirical AI research outcomes: replication status check
finding: Gap 10. The Wen test set needs at least one idea published after the GPT-4.1 cutoff (1 June 2024). Prompted models are near chance (GPT-4.1 51.9%) and the system reaches 63.6%. No later-cutoff or different-field replication of this exact test was found in the sources opened this session. Tong et al. (d03) uses a different method and test set, so it supports but does not replicate Wen.
numbers: Wen: GPT-4.1 51.9%, system 63.6% (earlier evidence c05). Tong: 1,000 pairs from 8,830, temporal and field-OOD tests.
limits: WebSearch budget ran out before a targeted replication search; absence of a found replication is not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: Keep K06 as established for trained judges across two groups with different labels (outcome vs citations), but flag that no like-for-like replication of the Wen test was found.

source: Foster et al. (2026) AI Research Preference Models: oracle gap arithmetic
finding: With all candidates scored, an oracle selector reaches 0.748 to 0.759, so a perfect picker adds at most about 0.06 to 0.07 over the unguided 0.684. The two RPMs recover about 42% and 70% of the validation-oracle gain.
limits: Shares computed by this agent from the paper's reported values. The oracle is bounded by the candidates the agent proposes.
agent_relevance: Gives a size for the S0 prize: selection can only recover what generation supplies, so expect a few percent on a mature task.

finding: An automated executor turns ideas into code and runs them, so selection and RL can use real outcomes. Model-based search with execution beats baselines, but RL on execution reward raises the average and not the maximum, and idea diversity collapses.
numbers: Execution rate over 90% (Claude-4.5 Sonnet/Opus self-executing) vs 42 to 78% under a GPT-5 executor. Post-training task: 69.4% vs 48.0% baseline and 68.8% best human. Pre-training: 19.7 min vs 35.9 baseline (best human 2.1 min). RL average reward 0.253 to 0.343 (GRPO) and 0.194 to 0.246 (nanoGPT); max reward flat. Diversity: 51 of 128 ideas were one of 2 common ideas at epoch 0, 119 of 128 at epoch 68.
limits: Only the first 100,000 of 203,000 characters read. Small-scale tasks. No LLM-predicted vs executed correlation reported. Only effectiveness rewarded.
agent_relevance: Execution outcome is the clean selector at small scale. Optimising the picker collapses variety, so the agent needs an explicit diversity or novelty term in S0.
